title: Critiquing the Rising Cities Ad
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter is about a single artifact rather than a technique: a full-page newspaper advertisement headlined "Rising Cities" that Stat 243's unit on graphics hands students as a critique exercise. It assumes you already have the unit's list of good practices for statistical graphics, and uses this one example to see what a real, professionally produced graphic looks like when it breaks several of those rules at once. ## Where the example sits in the course The course's "Graphics" unit states a working list of good practices for building a statistical graphic, then gives students a numbered list of real graphics to weigh against that list. This advertisement is one of them, described there as "an example of a crazy pie chart from an advertisement in the New York Times from December 2014." The same page — same wording, same three extracted images — is linked unchanged from at least three offerings of the course: 2021, 2024 and 2025. Whatever point the instructor makes with it, it has been worth making for years without needing a different example. The file name in the archive, `shell.pdf`/`shell.md`, is a leftover of how it was filed and has nothing to do with a Unix shell: it sits in the graphics unit's folder of supplementary readings, alongside a Wainer (1984) paper on how to display data badly and a Gelman and Unwin (2013) paper contrasting infographics with statistical graphics — two other critique readings from the same unit. ## What the advertisement shows The source PDF has no text layer, so what survives is a reconstruction of the words on the page, together with three images extracted from it. Put together, the page reads as follows. A full-bleed photograph of a city street at dusk, skyscrapers silhouetted against the sky, sits behind everything else. Over it, in large pale type, runs the headline "RISING CITIES," followed by a lead statistic: "The population of the world's cities will increase by 2.7 billion by 2050. Nearly 90% of this growth will take place in Asia and Africa." Below that sits a chart caption, "Share of worldwide urban population growth from 2010-2050, by region." The chart itself, visible in the extracted page image, is not a flat pie but a three-dimensional exploded one: wedges of a cylinder, drawn with visible side faces and shading, pulled apart from a common centre. The wedges that survive legibly on the scan carry only bare percentages — 1%, 3%, 9%, 11% — with no region name attached to any of them. The region names are given instead in a separate list printed elsewhere on the page: - 29% Sub-Saharan Africa - 18% India - 17% Other Asia & Oceania - 13% China - 11% Americas - 8% Middle East and N. Africa - 3% Europe - 1% Others These sum to 100%, so the chart is a complete partition of "worldwide urban population growth" — though nothing on the chart itself tells the reader that. The rest of the page is advertising rather than data: a prompt aimed at the newspaper reader rather than at the numbers — "Discover more on mobile — Download Blippar App — Fill Screen With Page — Experience the Future!" (Blippar was an augmented-reality app of the period; the invitation was to point a phone at the printed page to unlock further content). Who commissioned the advertisement, and what that further content was, is not recoverable from the material supplied. Below the chart run several paragraphs of copy on urbanization — that cities were, until about 2007, a minority way of living; that megacities are now growing fastest in Asia and Africa; that denser cities are also where growth, energy use and resource consumption concentrate — included here only because it is what the page actually says, not because it is itself a claim to check. ## Reading it against the course's own checklist Several items from the unit's "good practices" checklist apply directly to this page: - **Avoid 3-D graphics unless they truly add information.** Depth is the whole visual idea of this chart — the wedges are extruded and shaded to look like a drum sliced apart — but nothing about the depth encodes a value. Every wedge has the same height; only its angle carries data. - **Position or length compares better than area, volume or angle.** A flat pie chart is already a poor way to let a reader rank eight shares; an exploded, three-dimensional pie is harder still, because perspective distorts the apparent angle of the far side of the "drum" relative to the near side. - **Label the data on the graphic, and use a legend where it helps.** The visible wedges carry bare numbers with no region name attached to them; matching a wedge to "Middle East and N. Africa" or to "Europe" means cross-referencing a list printed elsewhere on the page. - **Show the data clearly.** The chart and the headline both compete with the full-bleed photograph behind them; parts of the "RISING CITIES" headline are themselves hard to read where the type sits over the darker parts of the picture. - **Have a high density of information to space.** A full newspaper page is spent on eight numbers. None of this means the advertisement failed at what it was built to do. The same unit's other reading, Gelman and Unwin (2013), draws a distinction between "information visualization" — built to attract attention and provoke interest — and "statistical graphics" — built to let a reader read off and compare values. Judged as the first, a striking three-dimensional chart on a moody photograph, with a phone prompt inviting the reader to go further, is doing exactly its job. Judged as the second, it fails: a reader cannot come away from the page able to say which of the eight regions contributed more to urban growth than which other, without leaving the chart to consult the list of numbers next to it. This is the same tension the course draws out elsewhere in the same unit with Florence Nightingale's coxcomb plot — a graphic can be excellent by one of these two goals and poor by the other, and the two are worth telling apart before judging a chart at all. ## The same numbers, redrawn Applying the checklist's own advice — use position or length from a shared baseline, rather than angle or volume — the same eight shares can be drawn as an ordinary horizontal bar chart instead. This does not do anything the advertisement's designers did not already know how to do; it only shows the size of the change in readability that "use length, not angle" buys on the same eight numbers. ## Sources - The chapter's given material: three copies of the same PDF, each reconstructed by a model because the PDF carries no text layer -- `units/graphics_files/shell.pdf` (berkeley-stat243 fall-2025, CC BY 4.0, converted 2026-09-18) and the same file in fall-2024 (CC BY 4.0), plus `units/shell.pdf` in stat243-fall-2021 (CC0-1.0). The three reconstructed texts are identical, which is itself the evidence that the instructor reused this example unchanged across years. Per each conversion's own caveat, this is a model's reconstruction of a PDF with no usable text layer -- the marketing copy and even the eight percentages above should be treated as unverified against the original printed page, not as citable numbers. - The three page images that each `shell.md` embeds (`shell/figures/p001-1.jpeg`, `p001-2.png`, `p001-5.png`), viewed directly to check what the "chart" pictured actually is -- a three- dimensional exploded pie drawn over a photograph, on what is recognisably a scanned newsprint page. - For why this example is in the course at all, and which checklist it is meant to be read against: `units/unit12-graphics/01-1-good-practices-for-graphics.md` (berkeley-stat243 fall-2025, CC BY 4.0, losslessly converted from the course's own `.qmd`). This file is not itself one of this chapter's listed inputs, but it is the immediate sibling page that links to this exact file as item 5 of its "Some example graphics" list, supplies the "crazy pie chart ... New York Times ... December 2014" description quoted above, and states the "best practices" checklist used in the critique. Its item 7 points to the Gelman and Unwin (2013) reading referenced above by name only. - What the lecture referred to but did not contain: the class discussion itself. The good-practices page poses each numbered example as an open question for discussion ("what do you like or not like ..."); no transcript or recording of what was actually said about this particular advertisement, in any of the three years it was assigned, was supplied.
